body_text:
The Riemann Hypothesis.

Every nontrivial zero $\rho$ of the Riemann zeta function satisfies:
$$ \operatorname{Re}(\rho) = \frac{1}{2}. $$

That is, all non-trivial zeros lie precisely on the critical vertical line $\operatorname{Re}(s) = 1/2$.

*Significance for Prime Number Distribution*:
The Prime Number Theorem—proved independently by Jacques Hadamard and Charles Jean de la Vallée Poussin
in 1896—is equivalent to the non-vanishing of $\zeta(s)$ on the boundary line $\operatorname{Re}(s) = 1$:
$$ \pi(x) \sim \operatorname{li}(x) = \int_2^x \frac{dt}{\ln t}. $$
In 1901, Helge von Koch proved that the Riemann Hypothesis is mathematically equivalent to the
sharpest possible square-root error bound in the Prime Number Theorem:
$$ \pi(x) = \operatorname{li}(x) + O(\sqrt{x} \ln x). $$
In this sense, the Riemann Hypothesis asserts that the primes are distributed as uniformly and
randomly as quantum noise around their smooth logarithmic integral trend.

*Deep Connections across Mathematics*:
The spacing of the zeros on the critical line exhibits statistical correlations identical to
the eigenvalues of random Hermitian matrices in the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (Montgomery's Pair
Correlation Conjecture and Freeman Dyson, 1972). This striking connection suggests the *Hilbert--Pólya
conjecture*: that the imaginary parts of the nontrivial zeros correspond to the eigenvalues of a
self-adjoint Hamiltonian operator in quantum mechanics.
